cells: Further, the current level of capital expenditure (capex) on AI infrastructure may not be sustainable over the long term and a significant reduction in AI-related spending will likely harm our financial results.
In addition, rapidly evolving technologies, including AI, could change the business needs of our customers in the data center and communications markets in ways we are not yet able to predict.

Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (“AI”) and machine learning (“ML”) technologies, including generative AI, could fundamentally alter the semiconductor industry and disrupt our business model and operations.

AI-driven tools and platforms are increasingly being deployed across the integrated circuit (“IC”) development lifecycle, including in chip architecture design, electronic design automation (“EDA”), layout optimization, verification, testing, and process node development.

AI-driven design tools may lower traditional barriers to entry in the semiconductor industry by enabling new market participants, including technology companies that have not historically engaged in chip design, to develop high-performance, custom semiconductor solutions in-house with reduced reliance on third-party chip suppliers.

In particular, large cloud computing providers, automotive original equipment manufacturers, and other technology-focused enterprises have already begun investing in proprietary chip design capabilities, and advancements in AI may accelerate this trend.

AI and ML technologies may enable our existing competitors to achieve design and manufacturing efficiencies that we are unable to match, thereby diminishing or eliminating our current technological or cost advantages.

Competitors that more effectively integrate AI into their IC development workflows may be able to bring products to market faster, at lower cost, or with superior performance characteristics compared to our offerings.

AI-generated efficiencies may compress product development cycles across the industry, which could shorten the useful commercial life of our existing products and reduce the return on our research and development investments.

As AI tools enable more rapid iteration and optimization of chip designs, customers may expect faster product refresh cycles, placing additional pressure on our research and development resources and potentially leading to accelerated inventory obsolescence.
Our investment in AI-related capabilities may not yield the anticipated benefits.

Developing, acquiring, or integrating AI-driven tools and talent into our operations will require significant capital expenditures and operational resources, and there is no assurance that these investments will generate a return sufficient to justify their cost.

Expert Takeaways: TSMC 1. CoWoS Capacity, Fab Breakdown, Spill‑Over Orders & Customer Allocation Capacity Expansion: TSMC's internal CoWoS monthly capacity is targeted to reach 130k wafers by end-2026, with a long-term goal of 260k wafers/month by 2028 (excluding OSAT volumes). Demand Growth: Market demand for CoWoS has increased by at least 26% compared to early-2026 levels. Fab Breakdown: AP8 full capacity is 50k wafers (>40k expected by end-2026); AP7-P1 reached its 35k full-load target after ramping in August; AP7-P2 focuses primarily on SoIC; US AP1 will not ramp significantly by year-end; legacy AP1–AP6 fabs handle the remaining volume. Expansion Bottlenecks: New packaging fab construction takes about three years from groundbreaking to bottleneck-limited full output, constrained mainly by hybrid bonding and 3–4 nm-grade CMP flatness requirements. OSAT Spill-Over Strategy: Lower-margin orders are routed to external OSATs (ASE, SPIL, Amkor) under signed LTAs, reserving TSMC’s internal capacity for high-value customers. Customer Allocation Split: Nvidia (60%), Broadcom (15%), AMD (10%), Marvell (6%), AWS in-house silicon (5%), MediaTek (2%), and others (3%). 2. SoIC Capacity Roadmap, Capital Intensity, Fab Bottlenecks & End‑Use Drivers Capacity Roadmap: Targeted at 15k wafers/month by end-2026, 24–28k by end-2027, and up to 45k by end-2028 (~90% CAGR in 2027). Capital Intensity & Bottlenecks: Capital intensity is $6.8–7.0 billion per 10k monthly wafers. Hybrid-bonding pick-and-place tools are the initial bottleneck, shifting dynamically to PVD and PECVD. Manufacturing Limits: High CMP flatness and particle cleanliness requirements create a hardware ceiling below CoWoS scale. Capacity is concentrated at Chiayi AP7 through end-2027 (long-term potential 40–50k/month). US AP1 will take future volume but faces a long learning curve requiring Taiwan team transfer. Key Demand Drivers: Nvidia (Rubin Ultra / Feynman), AMD (MI400 / Venice), Apple (M5 Pro / Max), and Broadcom ASICs slated for 2027. 3. Competitive Landscape (Intel / Samsung), Yields & Risk Mitigation Intel EMIB-T Status: Yield estimates vary from ~90% (supply chain) to 38–40% (test-vehicle data). EMIB-T die cost is ~50% of CoWoS-L. Intel outsources all backend assembly to Amkor across Longtan, Portugal, and Arizona. Samsung & Competitor Scale: Samsung I-Cube yield maturity lags peers, with meaningful competitive threats unlikely until post-2030 when hybrid bonding matures. Overall, TSMC’s advanced packaging volume is ~5× that of Intel. Customer De-Risking: Google is validating EMIB-T as a backup due to TSMC tightness, costs, and US policy. Broadcom is evaluating EMIB-T and Samsung capacity, while building a joint substrate/FC-BGA facility in Singapore with Toppan. 4. CoPoS Technical Bottlenecks, Production Timeline & Silicon Utilization Realistic Timeline: Mass CoPoS production in 2027–2028 is overly optimistic. AP7 has started qualification, aiming for limited NPI in 2027, low-volume production (LVM) for Nvidia Feynman in H2-2028, and true high-volume manufacturing (HVM) in 2029–2030. Glass-core TGV technology is deferred to post-2030. Technical Challenges: Five core bottlenecks include substrate warpage, fine-pitch RDL lithography, coat-and-plate uniformity, ~70% copper-fill yield for TGV vias, and large-format panel-tool standardization. Fab Footprint & Wafer Efficiency: US AP2 is provisionally planned for CoPoS. CoPoS requires greenfield fabs and won't cannibalize CoWoS. For large die sizes (e.g., 75×75 mm), CoPoS panel utilization reaches >84%, compared to just 48% on 12-inch circular wafers. 5. TSMC Co-Development Model & CPO Technology Outlook Deep Joint Development: Advanced packaging is not off-the-shelf; TSMC collaborates closely with key customers on architecture, process flow, equipment limits, photomasks, and probe cards (e.g., scaling SpaceX probe sites from 4–6 up to 32up). CPO Reality: Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) is not inherently tied to glass and can be built on silicon stacks. Key factors for success are I/O alignment precision and yield parity with CoWoS. Glass-based CPO currently faces high warpage and fracture risks. 6. Capital Expenditure, HPC Exposure & OSAT Dynamics CapEx Upside: TSMC total capex guidance was revised up from $52–56B to $60–64B, with ~10% allocated to backend packaging (CoWoS/SooS). Revenue Exposure: High Performance Computing (HPC) accounted for 68% of TSMC's Q3 revenue. OSAT Role: External OSAT capacity serves purely as supplementary volume and cannot replace TSMC’s core leadership in high-end advanced packaging. 7. New-Fab Constraints, Capacity Methodology & Portfolio Strategy Capacity Definition: Advanced-packaging fab capacity is defined by dynamic bottleneck tool stations (lithography, develop, die-bond, hybrid-bond) rather than physical floor space, creating variable output profiles across fabs. A9/A10 & Future Fabs: Insider visibility on A9/A10 schedules remains limited with no firm dates. Strategy: TSMC routes low-margin work externally while shifting internal capital toward next-gen CoPoS. Hybrid bonding and CMP flatness will remain recurring bottlenecks as Nvidia Feynman and HBM4-E ramp. 8. Supply-Chain Frictions from Constrained CoWoS-S Capacity CoWoS-S Shortages: Shifted focus toward CoWoS-L has left CoWoS-S expansion constrained, weighing on 2026 customer deliveries. Impacted Programs: TPU v7 / v8t implementations relying on CoWoS-S continue to face supply headwinds. Alternative Approaches: Broadcom’s Sunfish uses CoWoS-L and is positioned well for 2027. Broadcom v8t and Humu-fish evaluated EMIB-T as an alternative, but yields remain inadequate, keeping supply pressure high on CoWoS-S programs. $TSM $AVGO $GOOGL $NVDA $AMD $MRVL

blocks.text: Marvell Technology, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides data infrastructure semiconductor solutions and spanning the data center core to network edge in the United States, Argentina, China, India, Israel, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, and internationally. The company develops and scales system-on-a-chip architectures, integrating analog, mixed-signal, and digital signal processing functionality. It offers a portfolio of ethernet solutions, including spanning controllers, network adapters, physical transceivers, and switches; single or multiple core processors; and custom application specific integrated circuits, interconnects, fibre channel adapters, and processors. The company also provides interconnect products, including pulse amplitude modulation, coherent and coherent-lite digital signal processors (DSPs), laser drivers, trans-impedance amplifiers, silicon photonics, co-packaged optics, linear pluggable optics chipsets, data center interconnect, active electrical cable DSPs and peripheral component interconnect express retimer solutions; fibre channel products comprising host bus adapters and controllers for server and storage system connectivity; storage controllers for hard disk drives and solid-state-drives; host system interfaces, including serial advanced technology attachment and serial attached SCSI, peripheral component interconnect express, compute express link switches, non-volatile memory express (NVMe), and NVMe over fabrics; and develops ultra accelerator linkTM switches and ethernet for scale-up networking switches. The company serves data centers, communications, and other markets. It offers its products through direct customers and distributors. Marvell Technology, Inc. was incorporated in 1995 and is headquartered in Wilmington, Delaware.
